key_insight: Machine-learned long-time simulations show that small polarons at oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move far less than in bulk because surface geometry removes most efficient hopping pathways.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can exhibit lower electron mobility than single crystals, informing surface engineering for catalysts, photovoltaics, and energy-storage devices.
method: Extended a machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics framework to a reducible oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways and vacancy-driven free-energy changes.
evidence_signal: Several nanoseconds of simulation across multiple temperatures revealed polaron mobility at the reduced TiO2(110) surface is suppressed by orders of magnitude relative to bulk, with hopping mostly confined to inter-row motion in the second topmost layers.
watch_item: Transferability may still depend on the quality of the training data and on whether the learned model captures rare vacancy-mediated charge-transfer events at other oxide surfaces.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
